messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Question: beginner's resources
parts:
Hi all,

A quick request: I'm compiling some resources for an update to the website, and I'd like to get people's input.

What were the most useful resources for you when you started learning R?

I'm especially interested in specialized resources. For instance, if you started using R because you needed a specific method/test, what did you use to learn?

Thanks,

Noam

best,
Michele

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Question: beginner's resources
parts:
Great idea. I'm excited to see the compilation. Obviously, Google is your best friend. For all my even remotely common issues, there's a stackoverflow discussion. I find copying code to a temporary script and working through it while referring back to the discussion to understand what's going on pretty reliably good instruction. I found Richard's book examples tremendously useful for learning how to work with vectors and apply functions, write functions, make more advanced plots, etc. Introduction to Statistical Learning (also available for free online) also teaches through R examples -- I find that a very good way to learn both the statistical principles and the coding. 

-- 
Michael Levy

messages.author: 2083d5dd75475d0e
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Question: beginner's resources
parts:
I learned a good bit on working with, analyzing, and visualizing data in R using plyr (dplyr nowadays), reshape(2), and ggplot2 and their manuals, vignettes (http://had.co.nz/).

The link below contains lots of helpful tidbits on controlling (gg)plot features:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki

Also, for those with some database background, the sqldf package might be helpful for wrangling data into shape (https://code.google.com/p/sqldf/).

http://trinkerrstuff.wordpress.com/2013/05/19/sharing-my-r-notes/: you can download a 274 page pdf on the author's very detailed notes from learning R.

Finally, http://kbroman.github.io/hipsteR/ looks like a good reference for folks that might want a refresher on different ways to work with R.

messages.author: 52716a27c42802c7
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Question: beginner's resources
parts:
Thanks Bonnie!

I based the outline of the class mainly on Zuur's book "Beginner's Guide to R" which you can get electronically from our library. I think it gives a great overview of the basic workings of R and simple/ ubiquitous functions. Plus there is enough code in the book and also posted on his website (http://www.highstat.com/book3.htm)  that you can use Michael's recommendation and copy the code to follow along with the book's content. I've also found several other books by Zuur to be helpful in understanding both the R code and the theory behind the statistics (for me, mostly GLMMs and GAMs, incl zero inflation) - I think the writing is accessible to non-statisticians but still pretty thorough.

I've also found that many basic books don't really address the packages and tools for working with times in R. Here is a link that I think does a good job reviewing this sometimes critical aspect: http://www.stat.berkeley.edu/classes/s133/dates.html

Anna
